summary: Spiny, big-headed, structure-loving bottom fish caught as a bonus around wharves and flounder grounds across NB/NS/PEI — several similar species covered under one common name, none of them a dedicated target but all good fun on light bait gear.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
"Sculpin" in this region covers a handful of related, similar-looking bottom fish, most commonly the **grubby** (*Myoxocephalus aenaeus*) and **longhorn sculpin** (*Myoxocephalus octodecimspinosus*), with shorthorn sculpin (*Myoxocephalus scorpius*) also present in some areas. All share the classic sculpin body plan: an oversized, heavily armored/spined head relative to a tapering body, large fan-like pectoral fins, and a mottled brown/olive camouflage pattern that blends into rock and mud bottom.

The easiest field mark to tell grubby and longhorn apart: longhorn sculpin have long cheek spines, while the grubby's are noticeably short ("short-horned" by comparison) — useful if you want to know exactly which sculpin you've caught, though for fishing purposes they're targeted and handled identically. Longhorn sculpin specifically are common on Banquereau and Sable Island Banks offshore and throughout the **Bay of Fundy and St. Mary's Bay** inshore.

sources.label: Friends of Merrymeeting Bay, Longhorn sculpin
Friends of Merrymeeting Bay, Shorthorn sculpin

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md: Sculpin are present essentially year-round in their preferred structure and are not a run-timed or seasonal species the way gaspereau or smelt are. In practice, most anglers encounter them as an incidental catch while targeting winter flounder or fishing bottom bait near wharves, rather than fishing for them on purpose — so "when to go" is really just whenever you're already bottom-fishing.

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
Sculpin favour rocky, ledge-adjacent, or mixed mud/sand/pebble bottom in shoal water, plus the same shallow estuary flats that hold winter flounder.

- **NS:** The **Bay of Fundy and St. Mary's Bay** are noted longhorn sculpin habitat — St. Mary's Bay even supported a small directed commercial longhorn sculpin fishery (a short spring season, limited to a handful of licence holders) in past years, a sign of how common they are there. Cape Breton wharves also produce sculpin as bycatch while jigging for flounder.
- **NB:** Cocagne Cove specifically lists "grubby sculpin" among its notable catches; deeper channels of the Cocagne and Shediac estuaries are good bets generally.
- **PEI:** Shares habitat with winter flounder across Boughton Bay and the Three Rivers estuary — shallow, clear estuary bottom.

Any wharf, breakwater, or flounder ground across all three provinces is worth a look for sculpin as a bonus species.

sources.label: DFO, Assessment of St. Mary's Bay Longhorn Sculpin

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Rod | Same light spinning setup used for flounder/bottom fishing — 6-6'6" ML rod. |
| Rig | Hi-lo bottom rig, or a small soft plastic on a jighead for sight-fishing in clear shallows. |
| Bait | Small bait strips (clam, worm, cut fish) fished on or near bottom. |
| Handling gear | A rag or gloves — sculpin have sharp spines on the head and gill covers that can prick bare hands. |

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body_md:
1. Fish the same hi-lo bottom rig used for winter flounder, in and around rocky structure, ledges, or shallow estuary flats.
2. Slow retrieve with pauses on bottom — expect sculpin as an incidental bite alongside flounder, tomcod, and cunner.
3. In shallow, clear water, sculpin can also be **sight-fished**: spot a fish holding on bottom, drop a small bait-tipped jig close by, and let it settle — sculpin will lunge at a presentation placed right near them rather than chasing anything at distance.
4. No special retrieve needed beyond getting the bait in front of the fish; sculpin are opportunistic ambush feeders, not active hunters.

sources.label: Friends of Merrymeeting Bay, Longhorn sculpin

sections.heading: Handling & Release
sections.body_md: Sculpin have sharp spines on the head, gill covers, and dorsal fin that can jab an unwary hand — use a rag, glove, or grip behind the head/spines when unhooking. They also puff up and can flare their large pectoral fins and gill covers dramatically when handled, which is harmless but startling the first time you see it. Most anglers release sculpin given their small size and bony build; they handle release well and swim off strongly once returned to the water.

sections.heading: Conservation Notes
sections.body_md: No at-risk status turned up for either grubby or longhorn sculpin in this research. A small directed commercial fishery for longhorn sculpin has existed in St. Mary's Bay, NS (a short spring season limited to a handful of licence holders), indicating a locally healthy population there. No recreational bag limit turned up in current DFO notices for either species across NB/NS/PEI — treat as an abundant bonus species.

sources.label: DFO, Assessment of St. Mary's Bay Longhorn Sculpin

variants.name: Grubby
variants.how_to_tell: The smallest and shortest-spined of the region's common sculpins — cheek (preopercular) spines are noticeably short compared to longhorn sculpin's long, gill-cover-spanning spine, and grubby has only 10-11 anal fin rays with no pore behind the last gill arch (shorthorn has 13-14 rays and that pore).
variants.where_found: Same wharf, estuary, and flounder-ground bottom as the other sculpins region-wide, including Cocagne Cove, NB.
variants.notes: Least likely of the group to cause a painful spine wound given its short spines, but still worth a rag or glove when unhooking.

variants.name: Longhorn Sculpin
variants.how_to_tell: Identified by its long preopercular (cheek) spine, roughly four times the length of the spine below it and long enough to extend past the gill cover — the clearest single field mark separating it from grubby and shorthorn sculpin. Its first dorsal fin also stands taller than the second, and its lateral line shows smooth cartilaginous plates rather than the prickly scales found on shorthorn sculpin.
variants.where_found: Bay of Fundy and St. Mary's Bay, NS specifically, plus offshore on Banquereau and Sable Island Banks; also common inshore region-wide as flounder-ground bycatch.
variants.notes: Longhorn sculpin spines can inflict a genuinely painful puncture wound, with venom in the spine groove causing swelling, redness, and throbbing pain some anglers compare to a bee or wasp sting. Handle with a rag or glove, keep fingers clear of the head and gill-cover spines when unhooking, and immerse a puncture wound in hot water if stung.

variants.name: Shorthorn Sculpin
variants.how_to_tell: Cheek spines are short and blunt-triangular, with the uppermost less than twice the length of the one below it (versus longhorn's uppermost spine at roughly 4x). Shorthorn has 13-14 anal fin rays and a small pore on each side of the throat behind the last gill arch, both absent on grubby, and prickly (not smooth) scales along the lateral line versus longhorn's smooth cartilaginous plates.
variants.where_found: Same rocky, ledge, and estuary bottom as the other sculpins region-wide; tends toward colder, more northerly water within the group's range.
variants.notes: Spines are less prominent than longhorn's but still capable of a painful jab — same rag/glove handling applies.

variants.name: Sea Raven
variants.how_to_tell: Unmistakable once you know what to look for: sea raven has fleshy, branched skin tabs along the lower jaw, snout, and head, a ragged, torn-looking first dorsal fin outline unlike any true sculpin's, prickly spine-covered skin, and a stouter, heavier body than grubby, longhorn, or shorthorn sculpin.
variants.where_found: Same wharf and bottom structure as the other sculpins region-wide.
variants.notes: Not a true sculpin (a related but separate family, Hemitripteridae) — often lumped in with "sculpin" bycatch by anglers regardless. Handle carefully; the spiny skin and dorsal fin can still scrape or prick bare hands even without the venom concern longhorn sculpin poses.
